title: Math A Lecture 1: Mathematical Logic, Sequences and Series
sources: Mathematics with Statistics A – Lecture 1 (Prof. Dr. Enrico De Giorgi, 83 p.)
Book “Mathematics A”: ch. 2 (logic), ch. 6 (sequences), ch. 7 (series); E-MATHS.CH

bigPicture: Course goals: **formalise problems** in business and economics, **master and apply** mathematical techniques, develop **logical and critical thinking**.
**Logic:** propositions, the five logical operations and truth tables; **tautology** vs. **contradiction**; **proof by mathematical induction**.
**Sequences:** ordered lists {aₙ}; check **monotonicity, boundedness, convergence** (ε-definition). Bounded + monotone ⇒ convergent.
**Series:** sequences of partial sums. The **geometric series** sₙ = a₁(1 − qⁿ)/(1 − q) converges **iff |q| < 1** to **a₁/(1 − q)** – “the most useful result in this class”.

concepts.name: Statements, propositions and truth tables
concepts.simple: Maths works only with sentences that are clearly true or false. A truth table lists every combination and says when a new sentence is true.
exam: - A **statement** is “a formal written or oral account of facts, theories, opinions, events” (Oxford). A **proposition** is a statement that is clearly **either true (1) or false (0)**.
- “Yes we can” → not a proposition; “Enrico De Giorgi climbed Everest” → proposition, false; “This class is Mathematics A” → proposition, true.
- A **truth table** fully describes when a new proposition is true, depending on the values of the existing ones.
- D = “Ann, Bill AND Carl climbed Everest” is true **only** in the one row where A, B and C are all true (8 rows in total).
- The same logical operations appear in computer code (Python example).
concepts.example: “De Giorgi climbed Everest AND this class is Math A” is false; with OR it is true.

concepts.name: The five logical operations
concepts.simple: NOT flips, AND needs both, OR needs at least one (both is fine too), IMPLY only fails when the promise is broken, IFF needs both to agree.
exam: | A | B | ¬A | A ∧ B | A ∨ B | A ⇒ B | A ⇔ B |
| T | T | F | T | T | T | T |
| F | T | T | F | T | T | F |
| F | F | T | F | F | T | T |
- The mathematical OR is **inclusive**. **Exclusive OR = (A ∨ B) ∧ ¬(A ∧ B)** (true only in the rows T/F and F/T).

- **Implication** = a contract: “If Ann climbs Everest, then Bill pays Ann 100 000 CHF” is only violated when Ann climbs and Bill does not pay; if Ann does not climb, the contract is fulfilled whatever Bill does.
- **Equivalence**: Bill pays if **and only if** Ann climbs – paying although Ann did not climb makes A ⇔ B false (but A ⇒ B true).
- A ⇒ B: A is **sufficient** for B; A ⇔ B: A is **sufficient and necessary** for B.
- **¬(A ⇒ B) ⇔ A ∧ ¬B**: an implication is rejected by finding a case where A is true but B false (counterexample).
concepts.example: C = (A ∨ B) ∧ ¬(A ∧ B) is true exactly when one of A, B is true – the exclusive OR (“either… or…”).

concepts.name: Logic quiz: the three boxes
concepts.simple: Exactly one of the two clues is true. Try each case and see which one does not lead to a contradiction.
exam: Exactly one of three boxes contains 100 CHF. C = “The bill is in Box 1”, D = “The bill is not in Box 2”; at least one is true and at least one is false.
Reasoning: if C is true (Box 1), then D is also true → not allowed. So C is false and D must be true: not in Box 1 and not in Box 2 ⇒ **Box 3**.
concepts.example: Check: bill in Box 3 → C false, D true: exactly one true ✓.

concepts.name: Tautology and contradiction
concepts.simple: A tautology is always true whatever the parts are (‘to be or not to be’). A contradiction is always false (A and not A).
exam: - **Tautology:** a compound proposition **true in all cases**, e.g. **A ∨ ¬A** (“To be or not to be”).
- **Contradiction:** **false in all cases**, e.g. **A ∧ ¬A**.
- Tautology ↔ proof by mathematical induction; contradiction ↔ proof by contradiction.
concepts.example: Truth table of A ∨ ¬A: T, T. Of A ∧ ¬A: F, F.

concepts.name: Proof by mathematical induction
concepts.simple: Show it works for 1, and show ‘if it works for n, it works for n + 1’. Then it works for every n, like falling dominoes.
exam: Based on the tautology **[A ∧ (A ⇒ B)] ⇒ B**: if A and A ⇒ B are true, B must be true.
**Induction:** if A₁ is true and all implications Aₙ ⇒ Aₙ₊₁ are true, then Aₙ is true for all n.
**“All horses are of the same colour”** – a false induction proof; the slide asks: *where is the flaw?*
concepts.example: The horse flaw: the step Hₙ ⇒ Hₙ₊₁ fails for n = 1 (two horses: removing one leaves groups that do not overlap), so the chain of implications breaks.

concepts.name: Sequences: definition, explicit and recursive
concepts.simple: A sequence is a numbered list of numbers. You can give a formula for the n-th number, or a rule to get the next number from the previous one.
exam: **Definition:** a **sequence** is an ordered list {a₁, a₂, a₃, …} where each n ∈ ℕ corresponds exactly to a real number aₙ; written **{aₙ}ₙ∈ℕ**, n = index, aₙ = n-th term.
- **Order matters:** the same 20 numbers reordered follow yₖ = 2 cos(0.5k).
- **Recursive:** a₁ = 1, aₙ = ½(aₙ₋₁ + 3/aₙ₋₁).
- **Golden ratio:** (a + b)/a = a/b = **(1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618** equals lim aₙ₊₁/aₙ for the Fibonacci sequence.

concepts.name: Geometric sequences
concepts.simple: Each term is the previous one times the same number q (like interest: × 1.05 every year).
exam: **Definition:** {aₙ} is **geometric** if aₙ₊₁/aₙ = q is constant, q ∈ ℝ, q ≠ 0. Recursive aₙ₊₁ = aₙq ⇒ explicit **aₙ = a₁qⁿ⁻¹**.
Properties (a₁ ≠ 0):
- q > 0: monotone (a₁ > 0, q > 1 strictly increasing; a₁ > 0, 0 < q < 1 strictly decreasing; a₁ < 0 reverses this). q < 0: not monotone.
- Bounded for **|q| ≤ 1**, unbounded for |q| > 1.
- Convergent for **|q| < 1 (limit 0)** and **q = 1 (limit a₁)**; divergent for |q| > 1 and q = −1.
| Monotone | No | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Bounded | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Convergent | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
concepts.example: Invest 10 000 CHF at 5 % p.a.: capital at n = 20 is 10 000 · 1.05²⁰ ≈ 26 533 CHF.

concepts.name: Monotonicity and boundedness of sequences
concepts.simple: Increasing: each term is at least as big as the one before. Bounded: all terms stay between two fixed numbers.
exam: - **Increasing** if aₙ ≤ aₙ₊₁ ∀n (strictly: <); **decreasing** if aₙ ≥ aₙ₊₁ (strictly: >). Either one → **monotone**.
- **Bounded from above** if ∃M ∈ ℝ: aₙ ≤ M ∀n; **from below** if ∃m: aₙ ≥ m.
- **Bounded** if ∃c ∈ ℝ with |aₙ| ≤ c for all n.
concepts.example: aₙ = 1/n is strictly decreasing and bounded (0 < aₙ ≤ 1).

concepts.name: Limit of a sequence (ε-definition) and convergence theorems
concepts.simple: a is the limit if, however small a band you draw around a, from some point on all terms stay inside it.
exam: **Definition:** a ∈ ℝ (finite) is the **limit** of {aₙ} if for any ε > 0 there is n(ε) ∈ ℕ such that the distance between aₙ and a is smaller than ε for all n ≥ n(ε); we write a = lim_(n→∞) aₙ.
**Theorem:** a convergent sequence is (i) **bounded** and (ii) its limit is **unique**. Boundedness is **necessary**, not sufficient.
**Theorem:** **bounded + monotone ⇒ convergent**.
**Attention:**
- bounded AND divergent: aₙ = cos(n);
- monotone AND divergent: aₙ = n²;
- convergent AND non-monotone: aₙ = (−1)ⁿ/n.
concepts.example: aₙ = 1 − 1/n: increasing and bounded above by 1 ⇒ convergent, limit 1.

concepts.name: Partial sums and series
concepts.simple: A series is the running total of a sequence: s₁ = a₁, s₂ = a₁ + a₂, and so on. The infinite sum is the limit of these running totals.
exam: **Definition:** sₙ = a₁ + ⋯ + aₙ = Σₖ₌₁ⁿ aₖ is the **n-th partial sum**; the sequence {sₙ} is a **series**; sₙ = sₙ₋₁ + aₙ.
- **Harmonic series:** aₖ = 1/k: s₁ = 1, s₂ = 3/2, s₃ = 11/6.
- Series are sequences; the key question is **convergence**: if s = lim sₙ exists, we write s = Σₖ₌₁^∞ aₖ.
- **Marathon example:** speed 20 km/h in hour 1, −10 % each hour (aₖ₊₁ = 0.9aₖ); the distance after n hours is sₙ.
concepts.example: Total output growing 5 % p.a. over 10 years: O₀ + O₁ + ⋯ + O₁₀ = Σₖ₌₀¹⁰ O₀(1.05)ᵏ – a geometric series with q = 1.05.

concepts.name: Geometric series: closed form and convergence
concepts.simple: Adding up a geometric sequence has a shortcut formula. If |q| < 1 the infinite sum is finite: a₁/(1 − q).
exam: **Formula:** **sₙ = Σₖ₌₁ⁿ a₁qᵏ⁻¹ = a₁(1 − qⁿ)/(1 − q)** (q ≠ 1).
**Proof:** q·sₙ = a₂ + ⋯ + aₙ₊₁ ⇒ (1 − q)sₙ = a₁ − aₙ₊₁ = a₁(1 − qⁿ).
**Lemma (“the most useful result in this class”):** the geometric series converges **if and only if |q| < 1**, and then **Σₖ₌₀^∞ a₁qᵏ = a₁/(1 − q)**.
concepts.example: Marathon: lim sₙ = 20/(1 − 0.9) = **200 km** if she runs forever. After 2 h she has run 38 km, after 3 h 54.2 km → finishes 42.195 km between 2 and 3 h.

connections: **Pre-course 1** introduced the operators; Lecture 1 adds exclusive OR, tautologies and induction.
**Pre-course 2:** Σ-notation and Gauss' formula (proved here by induction).
**Pre-course 5:** limits of functions ↔ limits of sequences; the geometric sequence is exponential in n (Pre-course 4).
**Past exams (2011–2023)** regularly ask for the convergence of sequences and for which parameter a geometric series converges and its value.

questions: Build truth tables of compound propositions (e.g. exclusive OR).
Decide whether a sequence is monotone, bounded, convergent; compute the limit.
Recognise a geometric sequence/series; compute sₙ and the infinite sum; find parameter values for convergence.
traps: Bounded does **not** imply convergent (cos n); monotone does not imply convergent (n²).
Geometric series converges only for **|q| < 1** – q = −1 diverges.
Check the starting index: Σₖ₌₁ⁿ a₁qᵏ⁻¹ vs. Σₖ₌₀ⁿ⁻¹ a₁qᵏ (same sum).
In finance problems, n = 0 to 20 gives 21 terms.
mistakes: Writing aₙ = a₁qⁿ instead of a₁qⁿ⁻¹.

memorize: **Exclusive OR = (A ∨ B) ∧ ¬(A ∧ B); ¬(A ⇒ B) ⇔ A ∧ ¬B; (A ⇔ B) ⇔ (A ⇒ B) ∧ (B ⇒ A).**
**Induction:** A₁ true and Aₙ ⇒ Aₙ₊₁ ⇒ Aₙ true ∀n.
**Geometric sequence aₙ = a₁qⁿ⁻¹;** converges for −1 < q ≤ 1.

questions.question: Which sequence is bounded but divergent?
a₁ = −2, q = 1/2. The geometric sequence is…
Prove by induction that 1 + 2 + ⋯ + n = n(n + 1)/2 for all n ≥ 1.
questions.model:
Base case: n = 1: 1 = 1·2/2 ✓.
Induction step: assume 1 + ⋯ + n = n(n + 1)/2. Then 1 + ⋯ + n + (n + 1) = n(n + 1)/2 + (n + 1) = (n² + 3n + 2)/2 = (n + 1)(n + 2)/2, which is the formula for n + 1.
By induction the formula holds for all n ≥ 1.

questions.question:
A runner covers 20 km in the first hour; each hour her average speed drops by 10 %.
(a) Show that the hourly distances form a geometric sequence and give q.
(b) Give the formula for the distance sₙ after n hours and compute s₂ and s₃.
(c) Can she finish a marathon (42.195 km)? What distance would she reach if she ran forever?
questions.model:
(a) aₖ₊₁ = 0.9aₖ: constant ratio q = 0.9, a₁ = 20.
(b) sₙ = 20(1 − 0.9ⁿ)/(1 − 0.9) = 200(1 − 0.9ⁿ); s₂ = 38 km, s₃ = 54.2 km.
(c) Yes – she passes 42.195 km between hour 2 and 3. Since |q| < 1 the series converges: lim sₙ = 20/(1 − 0.9) = 200 km.
